lesson.title: One Mailbox, Every Device: How IMAP Keeps Email in Sync
lesson.summary: IMAP is the retrieval protocol that lets a client view and manage a mailbox that stays stored on the server, so read status, folders, and messages stay consistent no matter which device is used to check email.
lesson.body:
SMTP's job ends the moment a message is deposited into the recipient's mailbox on their mail provider's server. Getting that message from the server onto a screen where a person can actually read it is a separate problem, handled by a retrieval protocol, and IMAP, the Internet Message Access Protocol, is the retrieval protocol built around a specific idea: the mailbox lives on the server, and every client is just a window into it.

When an email client uses IMAP, it does not simply pull messages down and store them as the primary copy. Instead, it treats the server's mailbox as the source of truth. Folder structure, which messages exist, whether a message has been read, flagged, or deleted, all of that state lives on the server, and the client synchronizes with it. This is precisely why IMAP works so well for anyone who checks email from more than one device: open the same account on a phone, a laptop, and a web browser, and all three show the same folders, the same read and unread markers, and the same messages, because each client is reading and writing to the same server side state rather than keeping its own independent copy that could drift out of sync with the others.

IMAP also supports more selective interaction with a mailbox than simply downloading everything. A client can fetch just a message's headers to build a preview list without pulling down the full body or attachments, which matters on a slow connection or a device with limited storage, and can search, move messages between folders, or mark them in ways that get reflected back to the server for every other client to see. None of this requires copying the whole mailbox down to the device first.

Building on the previous chapter, it is worth restating the division of labor clearly: SMTP is the protocol responsible for sending a message and relaying it toward its destination, while IMAP is the protocol responsible for reading and organizing messages that have already arrived and are sitting in a mailbox. A typical email client uses both at once, SMTP to send outgoing mail and IMAP to display and manage incoming mail, and neither protocol does the other's job.
